qualifying_findings.title: GitLab 19.4.1, 19.3.3, and 19.2.7 patched Duo AI, Duo Workflow, and MCP authorization issues
visible_dates: NVD publication timestamps: 2026-09-24T00:17:22Z for CVE-2026-92470, CVE-2026-92529, CVE-2026-92628, and CVE-2026-92874
qualifying_findings.evidence_classification: primary vendor patch release corroborated by NVD CVE records
qualifying_findings.affected_boundary_or_version: GitLab CE/EE and EE ranges before 19.2.7, 19.3.3, and 19.4.1, depending on CVE.
qualifying_findings.summary: GitLab disclosed a patch release with four AI/MCP-relevant flaws: Duo AI troubleshooting could expose CI/CD variable values from debug-mode job traces; Duo Workflow Service token governance could be bypassed by a developer-role user in namespaces they did not control; MCP-scoped tokens could perform actions beyond intended scope; and the MCP gitlab_search tool could return search results under the wrong user context under a race condition.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: The patch cluster hits the exact boundaries this wiki tracks: AI troubleshooting access to secrets, AI workflow governance enforcement, scoped MCP token least privilege, and user-context isolation for agent search tools.

qualifying_findings.title: mcp-remote advisory cluster covered SSRF, authorization metadata disclosure, and remote code execution paths
qualifying_findings.affected_boundary_or_version: geelen mcp-remote versions 0.1.16 through 0.1.38 or 0.1.32 through 0.1.38, depending on CVE.
qualifying_findings.summary: NVD published five mcp-remote records covering SSRF through a resource_metadata URL in a remote MCP server WWW-Authenticate header, authorization-server metadata information disclosure, arbitrary code execution through server URL hashing and browser open paths, and SSE transport token-origin disclosure.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: Remote MCP clients ingest metadata and transport details from untrusted or semi-trusted remote servers; these flaws show how discovery, OAuth metadata, URL hashing, and browser-opening helpers can cross network, credential, and code-execution boundaries.

qualifying_findings.title: IBM ContextForge MCP Gateway 1.0.0 through 1.0.8 path traversal in Admin API log download
qualifying_findings.evidence_classification: primary vendor security bulletin with CVE corroboration
qualifying_findings.affected_boundary_or_version: IBM ContextForge MCP Gateway v1.0.0 through v1.0.8; fixed in v1.0.9 or later.
qualifying_findings.summary: IBM disclosed that an authenticated administrative user could exploit string-prefix path confinement in GET /v1/admin/logs/file to retrieve .log, .jsonl, and .json files from sibling directories outside LOG_FOLDER. IBM recommends upgrading to 1.0.9 or later and disabling the Admin API when administrative endpoints are not required.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: MCP gateways aggregate tool calls, logs, and credentials. Administrative log-read boundaries need real path confinement because log and JSONL files may contain tool requests, prompts, credentials, or audit evidence.

qualifying_findings.title: DBHub MCP server published critical HTTP DNS-rebinding and read-only enforcement advisories
visible_dates: GitHub Advisory Database published to GHSA and reviewed: 2026-09-24 for both advisories
qualifying_findings.evidence_classification: GitHub reviewed advisories with NVD corroboration and reproducible PoC detail
qualifying_findings.affected_boundary_or_version: @bytebase/dbhub before 0.22.5 for CVE-2026-61742; before 0.22.6 for CVE-2026-61788.
qualifying_findings.summary: DBHub's documented HTTP MCP transport exposed unauthenticated /mcp tool calls to DNS rebinding because Host and Origin equality was treated as trust. Separately, readonly=true on execute_sql did not actually enforce database-level read-only operation, so SELECT statements with side effects could mutate data, read host files, write files, or reach command execution with privileged PostgreSQL roles. Fixes landed in 0.22.5 and 0.22.6.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: Database MCP servers are high-impact delegated-authority surfaces. Browser-origin trust and model-facing read-only claims are not enough; dispatch must enforce auth, allowed origins/hosts, and database-level least privilege.

upstream_routing.security_local: Keep the DNS rebinding, unauthenticated HTTP MCP, and read-only enforcement failures here.
upstream_routing.ai_wiki: DBHub as an MCP server/tool entity belongs upstream if broad product coverage is needed.
upstream_routing.ai_dev_wiki: General database-tooling workflow guidance belongs upstream unless tied to security enforcement.

qualifying_findings.confidence_notes: High confidence. GitHub reviewed advisories include detailed impact, versions, references, and fixes.

qualifying_findings.title: Decepticon patched ChatML special-token role-boundary forgery leading to sandbox command execution
visible_dates: GitHub advisory updated, reviewed, and published to GitHub Advisory Database: 2026-09-24
qualifying_findings.evidence_classification: GitHub reviewed advisory with CVE record and reproduction details
qualifying_findings.affected_boundary_or_version: decepticon, decepticon-core, and decepticon-sdk <= 1.1.16; fixed in 1.1.17.
qualifying_findings.summary: Decepticon wrapped web crawl results into LLM messages without neutralizing ChatML special-token literals. In BYOK deployments using OpenAI-compatible backends that preserve special-token IDs, attacker-planted webpage content could forge a structural operator turn, bypass guardrails, and trigger arbitrary command execution inside the Kali Linux sandbox. The advisory recommends filtering or escaping special-token literals before composing untrusted external content into LLM messages.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: This is a concrete model-context integrity failure, not just generic prompt injection: untrusted tool output can become structural role metadata if the application layer does not neutralize tokenizer special tokens.

upstream_routing.security_local: Keep the special-token injection and command-execution boundary here.
upstream_routing.ai_wiki: Decepticon as a red-team agent product and model-provider background belong upstream if needed.
upstream_routing.ai_dev_wiki: General agent skill/tool-output handling practice belongs upstream only when not security-specific.

qualifying_findings.confidence_notes: High confidence from detailed reviewed advisory and CVE record.

qualifying_findings.title: TREK 3.3.0 fixed LLM base URL SSRF and MCP trip-summary scope bypass
qualifying_findings.summary: TREK allowed an authenticated trip writer to store an attacker-controlled llm_base_url that was later consumed by AI-assisted parsing clients without the intended SSRF guard, enabling internal-service or cloud-metadata access. Separately, the get_trip_summary MCP tool was registered for scoped OAuth MCP tokens without requiring trips:read, exposing trip metadata, member email addresses, itinerary days, and accommodations to an MCP client with unrelated scopes.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: The pair shows both sides of delegated AI data access: LLM provider URL routing must enforce SSRF controls, and MCP tool registration must enforce per-tool OAuth scopes rather than relying on broader user authorization.

upstream_routing.security_local: Keep LLM URL SSRF and MCP OAuth scope-bypass implications here.
upstream_routing.ai_wiki: TREK as a product/entity belongs upstream only if broad ecosystem coverage is needed.

qualifying_findings.title: OpenWA 0.23.5 fixed MCP invite-code role boundary failure
qualifying_findings.summary: OpenWA's GET invite-code endpoint and GroupGetInviteCode MCP tool lacked the intended OPERATOR role requirement. A VIEWER key scoped to a session could retrieve a transferable WhatsApp group invite code, letting an external account join and retain group access after the VIEWER key was revoked.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: MCP tools can mint or disclose bearer capabilities outside the application credential system; role checks must protect capability-producing tool calls, not only API sessions.

qualifying_findings.title: Rapid7 Bulk Export MCP 0.6.2 fixed tool-argument GraphQL query injection
qualifying_findings.affected_boundary_or_version: Rapid7 Bulk Export MCP versions 0.2.5 through 0.6.1; fixed in 0.6.2.
qualifying_findings.summary: The get_export_status path interpolated an unvalidated export_id MCP tool argument directly into a GraphQL query sent with the operator's Rapid7 API key. A crafted export_id could append additional root-level selections such as schema introspection. The fix parameterizes export_id as a GraphQL variable.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: Even when an injected query stays within the operator's own API scope, compromised MCP clients or indirect prompt injection can transform untrusted tool arguments into privileged API calls.

qualifying_findings.title: OpenClaw September 26 CVE cluster covered ACP file reads, command approval bypasses, MCP policy bypass, and owner authorization gaps
qualifying_findings.affected_boundary_or_version: OpenClaw npm package and runtime versions before 2026.7.1 or 2026.8.1 depending on CVE.
qualifying_findings.summary: NVD published an OpenClaw cluster spanning alternate file: URL path classification leading to out-of-workdir reads, escaped-newline command allowlist bypass, persistent Allow Always grants becoming path-only approvals, wrapper trust gaps, denied MCP tool invocation from sandboxed sessions, Claude Code permission prompt owner-check failures over the MCP bridge, non-owner computer-use plugin installation, trajectory export authorization bypass, and non-owner /mcp configuration changes that could persist stdio MCP commands.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: This is a broad delegated-authority cluster for coding agents: approval prompts, ACP file access, MCP tool policy, owner-only actions, and persisted MCP configuration all need independent authorization checks.

qualifying_findings.title: MCP Server for WordPress 1.8.2 fixed REST nonce, workflow ownership, and object authorization flaws
qualifying_findings.affected_boundary_or_version: MCP Server for WordPress plugin before 1.8.2; fixed in 1.8.2.
qualifying_findings.summary: The MCP Server for WordPress plugin had three in-window CVEs: REST API nonce verification could be bypassed for cookie-authenticated requests, allowing attacker-induced administrator actions including administrator account creation; Contributors could create, modify, or delete site-wide workflow configuration; and a workflow route lacked object-level authorization, exposing titles and publication status for private, draft, pending, and scheduled content.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: CMS-hosted MCP servers combine web CSRF/nonce semantics with agent workflow configuration; workflow and object authorization failures can turn low-privilege users or browser attacks into agent-control-plane changes.

qualifying_findings.title: SiYuan 3.8.4 fixed recursive MCP file sensitive-path guard bypass
qualifying_findings.summary: SiYuan applied the MCP file tool sensitive-path guard only to the allowed root of recursive operations, not each resolved descendant. An authenticated administrator using the in-app Agent or external MCP server could use file.grep, file.copy, or unzip to expose or overwrite protected descendants such as conf/conf.json, TLS keys, snippets, templates, notebook internals, or logs. Some actions were marked safe or had confirmation cards that hid descendant paths.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: Recursive file tools must enforce deny lists on every resolved path and show accurate approval evidence; otherwise apparently safe agent file actions can disclose credentials and configuration.

qualifying_findings.title: Zammad 7.1.2 fixed AI Agent command execution, analytics error disclosure, and admin UI XSS issues
qualifying_findings.summary: Zammad fixed an AI Agent configuration-filter bypass that allowed an administrator creating or editing AI Agents to run arbitrary server commands when the affected agent next processed a ticket. It also fixed an AI analytics run identifier authorization gap that disclosed provider error messages, plus unsanitized option labels rendered as raw HTML in AI Agent configuration dialogs.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: AI agent configuration fields are execution-adjacent policy surfaces. Admin-only does not eliminate the need for sandboxing and sanitization when the configuration later runs automatically in ticket-processing flows.

qualifying_findings.title: LiteLLM before 1.101.0-rc.1 disclosed cross-tenant cached responses and tool-call payloads
qualifying_findings.summary: LiteLLM's semantic cache had a tenant-isolation bypass caused by a metadata-key mismatch between tenant-scope calculation and metadata variable naming. Authenticated users with valid virtual keys could submit semantically similar prompts to retrieve other tenants' cached responses containing sensitive data, and agentic front ends could auto-execute cached function_call or tool_calls payloads under a different principal.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: Semantic caches are model-facing shared state. Tenant scoping must cover both text and tool-call payloads, because cached function calls can become delegated actions under the wrong identity.

upstream_routing.security_local: Keep cache tenant isolation and cross-principal tool-call replay implications here.

qualifying_findings.title: Flowise through 3.1.4 exposed chat histories and queue payloads through missing RBAC checks
qualifying_findings.affected_boundary_or_version: Flowise through 3.1.4; no patched version available for the BullMQ dashboard record as of the advisory text.
qualifying_findings.summary: Flowise allowed low-privileged API keys to read and delete chat history because chat-message endpoints lacked route-level RBAC. Separately, when queue mode and the BullMQ dashboard were enabled outside cloud mode, any authenticated user could access the dashboard without role, workspace, or organization scoping, exposing queues and job payloads including chat inputs, prompts, model responses, overrideConfig values, credential IDs, files, and workspace identifiers, with write actions also available.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: AI workflow builders hold prompts, model outputs, credentials, and queued jobs. Route-level RBAC and tenant scoping must apply to both normal APIs and operational dashboards.

upstream_routing.security_local: Keep chat-history RBAC and AI workflow queue dashboard exposure here.

qualifying_findings.title: vLLM 0.29.0 fixed multimodal decoder prompt-length validation DoS
qualifying_findings.summary: vLLM's disaggregated serving endpoint /inference/v1/generate failed to enforce decoder prompt-length validation when multimodal features were supplied. For processors such as Nemotron Parse, Whisper, and FireRedLID that skip prompt-length checks, an overlong token_ids list could reach a fixed max_model_len-wide worker buffer and crash the worker.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: Model serving endpoints need consistent prompt-length enforcement across multimodal and disaggregated paths; otherwise malformed requests can cause denial of service in inference workers.
